Cross-species recurrence graph of ortholog-group pairs

Source: R/recurrence_graph.R
recurrence_graph.Rd

Contracts each species' co-expression network to ortholog groups, counts in how many species every pair of groups is co-expressed, and tests that count against independence of the species. Significant pairs form a weighted graph over ortholog groups for recurrence_modules().

recurrence_graph(nets, hog_map, alpha = 0.05, min_species = 2L)

Arguments

nets

Named list of at least two network objects from compute_network(), one per species.

hog_map

Data frame with columns species, gene and hog, one row per gene copy (many-to-many). Genes outside a species' network are ignored.

alpha

FDR level for the edges of graph.

min_species

Smallest \(K\) for a pair to be tested.

Value

An object of class recurrence_graph: edges (data frame of the tested pairs: hog1, hog2, K, profile = presence per species in names(nets) order as a string such as "101", p.val, q.val), species (species, density, n_hogs, n_genes, over group-mapped genes in the network), copies (group x species integer matrix of copies in the network), graph (undirected igraph of the pairs with q.val < alpha, edge weight = -log10(p.val)), genes (named list, the network genes of each species) and params (with n_tests, the number of testable pairs BH corrects over).

Details

Contraction. In species \(s\) the binary adjacency \(A_s\) at net$threshold (membership only; edge weights are not read) is contracted to ortholog groups by \(M^T A_s M\), with \(M\) the gene-by-group indicator: the pair \((h_1, h_2)\), \(h_1 \ne h_2\), is present in \(s\) when any copy of \(h_1\) is a neighbour of any copy of \(h_2\). This is MULE's ortholog contraction (Koyuturk et al. 2004). Within-group pairs are not scored.

Null. With expression shuffled within each species, the species are independent and an edge of species \(s\) falls on a gene pair with probability \(d_s\), the realised edge density among the group-mapped genes. A pair whose groups have \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) copies in \(s\) is then present with probability \(p_s = 1 - (1 - d_s)^{c_1 c_2}\), so paralog copy number enters the probability, not a weight. The number of species \(K\) in which the pair is present is Poisson-binomial over the \(p_s\); p.val is the exact upper tail \(P(K \ge k_{obs})\) by iterative convolution. Only pairs with \(K \ge\) min_species are listed, but q.val is Benjamini-Hochberg over every pair whose groups share at least min_species species (params$n_tests), the unlisted ones counted at p = 1. Correcting over the listed pairs alone selects on the outcome: on three shuffled 200-gene networks at d = 0.03 every listed pair has p near \(3 d^2\), and that correction called all 73 of them at q < 0.05; the full count calls none. This is CODENSE's summary graph (Hu et al. 2005) with an analytic null. Within-species triangles make edges of one species dependent but leave each edge's marginal alone; on shuffled Pooideae leaf, root and EVOTREE wood networks (six to eight species, BH over the listed pairs) the null gave 0 pairs at q < 0.05 and matched the K distribution within 3 % at every K (dev/design-notes/module-engine-borrow-scope.md, Section 10.3).

References

Hu, H., Yan, X., Huang, Y., Han, J. & Zhou, X. J. (2005). Mining coherent dense subgraphs across massive biological networks for functional discovery. Bioinformatics, 21(Suppl 1), i213–i221. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/bti1049

Koyuturk, M., Grama, A. & Szpankowski, W. (2004). An efficient algorithm for detecting frequent subgraphs in biological networks. Bioinformatics, 20(Suppl 1), i200–i207. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/bth919
